notes: Permission to appeal on consequential JR orders in tobacco forfeiture case; Scott Baker LJ refused leave on remittal, costs and party status.

enrichment.short_title: Ward v Portsmouth Crown Court: permission to appeal on tobacco forfeiture JR orders
key_facts: Mr Ward and Mr Boxall arrived at Portsmouth with large quantities of cigarettes and tobacco; customs seized the goods and magistrates made condemnation orders.
Both appealed to the Crown Court; after Hoverspeed the High Court quashed Mr Boxall's Crown Court decision and remitted for retrial.
Mr Ward's separate judicial review succeeded in quashing the Crown Court decision and remitting to the magistrates, but Mr Justice Walker refused permission to appeal and made no order as to costs.
Mr Ward sought permission to challenge remittal, the striking out of interested parties, and the costs order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal against consequential orders in a successful judicial review of a Crown Court tobacco forfeiture decision.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; the main quashing order stood and peripheral challenges to remittal, party status and costs had no real prospect of success.
enrichment.ratio: Where a judicial review claimant obtains the substantive relief sought, permission to appeal will rarely be granted on peripheral orders such as remittal to the lower court, substitution of interested parties, or a no-order-as-to-costs decision within the judge's discretion.
legal_issues: Whether the case should have been remitted for retrial rather than final relief granted
Whether Customs and Excise were properly substituted as interested parties
Whether Mr Boxall should remain an interested party
Whether the claimant should have recovered costs
linked_authorities: R v Hoverspeed Ltd [2002] 3 WLR 1219

confidence.notes: Short permission judgment with clear refusal on each ground; background facts are fully narrated.

notes: Litigant-in-person custody and financial remedy permission applications; Scott Baker LJ refused leave on CAFCASS recording and second appeal points.

enrichment.short_title: Chauhan v Chauhan: permission to appeal family directions and financial orders
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Chauhan had three young children and long-running acrimonious proceedings after separation in 2001.
Judge Ticehurst ordered a further CAFCASS welfare report but refused Mr Chauhan's request to tape-record CAFCASS interviews.
District judges made attachment of earnings and variation orders in financial remedy proceedings; Judge Meston refused permission to appeal.
Mr Chauhan sought second appeal to the Court of Appeal alleging bias, gender discrimination and procedural unfairness.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications for permission to appeal case-management directions in children proceedings and refusals of permission to appeal financial remedy orders.
enrichment.outcome: Both applications refused; no real prospect of success on tape-recording CAFCASS interviews or on second appeal from circuit judge refusals.
enrichment.ratio: The Court of Appeal rarely interferes with interlocutory family directions such as refusal to order tape-recording of CAFCASS interviews, and a second appeal requires an important point of practice or procedure with a high threshold that was not met here.
legal_issues: Whether CAFCASS interviews should be tape-recorded and disclosed
Whether the judge's directions breached Articles 6, 8 or 14 ECHR
Whether district judge orders on attachment of earnings and periodical payments were plainly wrong
Whether permission for a second appeal should be granted

confidence.notes: Detailed permission judgment summarising extensive lower court history with clear refusals on each application.

notes: Interlocutory JR directions in compulsory psychiatric treatment case; Crane J granted permission and relisted substantive hearing.

enrichment.short_title: Taylor v Haydyn-Smith: directions in compulsory psychiatric treatment JR
key_facts: The claimant challenged compulsory psychiatric medical treatment by judicial review.
Cooke J had granted an interim injunction on 14 January 2005; Hodge J refused permission on the papers on 10 March and lifted the injunction.
Munby J gave further directions on 25 April 2005 and a new second doctor was certified on 30 April.
Scheduling difficulties prevented a two-day permission and substantive hearing proceeding; Crane J relisted for 24 May 2005.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Case management hearing in judicial review concerning compulsory psychiatric treatment, following earlier permission and injunction decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Claim form amendment permitted; permission granted against first and second defendants; substantive hearing fixed for 24 May 2005 with first defendant undertaking not to medicate compulsorily pending determination.
enrichment.ratio: Where an urgent psychiatric treatment judicial review cannot proceed on the listed date because witnesses are unavailable and parties were misled as to the nature of the hearing, the court may grant permission and relist a substantive hearing rather than apportion blame for the adjournment.
legal_issues: Whether permission for judicial review should be granted
Whether cross-examination of medical witnesses was required
Appropriate timetable for substantive hearing and further evidence
Interim restraint on compulsory medication pending trial

notes: Partnership life policy trust dispute; judge held proprietary estoppel but GA Policy counterclaim succeeded as partnership asset.

enrichment.short_title: Strover v Strover: partnership life assurance trust and proprietary estoppel
key_facts: David Strover retired from the accountants' partnership Strover Leader & Co in 1999 and continued paying premiums on a £100,000 Friends Provident policy written in trust for surviving partners.
On his death the default trust beneficiaries were the surviving partners John Strover and John Ironmonger, not his estate.
All parties mistakenly assumed that after retirement the policy remained for the deceased's own benefit if he maintained premiums.
A separate GA Policy taken out for an NWS loan was treated as a partnership asset.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of claim and counterclaim by personal representatives concerning proceeds of partnership life assurance policies after partner retirement and death.
enrichment.outcome: Proprietary estoppel held the FP Policy proceeds were effectively the deceased's, subject to a 20% discount; the GA Policy proceeds were held for the partnership including the deceased's estate.
enrichment.ratio: Where a retired partner continued policy premiums on the shared assumption that a life policy written in trust was for his benefit, surviving partners who knew of that assumption may be estopped from asserting strict trust rights; separate policies funded from partnership accounts may remain partnership assets on dissolution.
legal_issues: Whether the FP Policy trust should be rectified for retirement scenarios
Whether a constructive or resulting trust arose on partnership dissolution
Whether proprietary estoppel applied despite defective pleading
Whether the GA Policy was a partnership asset notwithstanding individual NWS loans
linked_authorities: Oxley v Hiscock [2004] EWCA Civ 546
Amalgamated Investment & Property Co Ltd v Texas Commerce International Bank [1982] 1 QB 84
Grant v Edwards [1986] 1 Ch 638
Jennings v Rice [2003] 1 P&CR 100

notes: Filobake samosa pastry line appeal; Court of Appeal widened performance warranty construction but dismissed on breach and damages.

enrichment.short_title: Filobake v Rondo: samosa pastry production line performance guarantee
key_facts: Filobake bought a Rondo thin pastry production line to manufacture samosa pastry, with a performance guarantee tied to an attached recipe.
After installation the line failed to produce acceptable samosa pastry at the specified speed and thickness when used with Frampton oven and cooler.
Filobake purported to reject the equipment and claimed substantial loss of profits; Seymour J dismissed the claim against Rondo.
Experts agreed the line could extrude dough at specification with adjusted water content and a spiral mixer.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Technology and Construction Court judgment dismissing claim for breach of express and implied terms in supply of pastry manufacturing equipment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; although the performance obligation was wider than the judge found, breach was not established and loss of profits and wasted expenditure claims failed.
enrichment.ratio: A performance warranty that equipment will produce samosa pastry to an attached recipe requires extruded pastry capable of commercial samosa use, not merely dimensional throughput; nevertheless expert evidence may show compliance and acceptance may defeat rejection and alternative Cullinane damages.
legal_issues: Construction of the performance guarantee and attached samosa recipe
Whether Rondo equipment was of satisfactory quality and fit for purpose
Whether Filobake had accepted the goods before purported rejection
Whether wasted expenditure could be claimed under Cullinane/Anglia principles

notes: Solicitor negligence appeal on section 459 petition advice; Carnwath LJ dismissed claim over Jewson valuation expectations.

enrichment.short_title: Wilks v Perkins Mainman: negligent advice on section 459 petition
key_facts: Mr Wilks, a 50% shareholder in Warwick Ltd, consulted solicitors after falling out with his co-director Mr Chadwick.
Leading counsel advised a good section 459 unfair prejudice case if dismissal allegations were unfounded.
Solicitors advised litigation was the only option after informal Jewson acquisition discussions; proceedings were issued then discontinued.
Mr Wilks claimed negligent advice that courts would take the unwritten Jewson offer into account in share valuation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from trial judgment dismissing professional negligence claim for abortive section 459 petition costs of about £15,000.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge was entitled to find the Jewson valuation advice was not given and the 'only option to litigate' point was not pursued at trial.
enrichment.ratio: The scope of a solicitor's duty of care depends on instructions and the client's characteristics; an experienced businessman who does not disclose his valuation expectations cannot blame solicitors for failing to disabuse him, and issues not pursued at trial need not be addressed on appeal.
legal_issues: Whether solicitors negligently advised that a third-party offer would affect share valuation
Whether advice that litigation was the only option was negligent
Whether solicitors should have warned about likely valuation range
Whether the 'no option but to litigate' issue was before the trial judge
linked_authorities: Pickersgill v Riley [2004] UKPC 14

confidence.notes: Full appellate reasoning on trial conduct, pleadings and credibility with clear dismissal.

notes: Copyright infringement costs permission application; Neuberger LJ granted leave to appeal £50k costs after £180 damages award.

enrichment.short_title: Brown v MCASSO Music: permission to appeal costs after copyright win
key_facts: Mr Locksley Brown succeeded at trial on copyright infringement but recovered only £180 damages after a four-day hearing.
HHJ Fysh ordered Mr Brown to pay the defendant's costs exceeding £50,000.
The judge relied on pre-action without prejudice offers of £450 in March 2003 and a December 2003 offer of costs each way.
In open court the defendant's representative said he wanted the court to decide the copyright issue on principle.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal a county court costs order following successful but low-value copyright infringement claim.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal on costs granted; prospects were modest but the defendant's open-court stance and post-issue settlement breakdown warranted appellate review.
enrichment.ratio: Even where a claimant succeeds on liability, a costs order based on pre-action offers requires careful analysis of without prejudice status and subsequent conduct; a defendant's stated desire for a court ruling on the principal issue may undermine reliance on settlement offers.
legal_issues: Whether pre-action without prejudice offers could be taken into account on costs
Effect of a March 2003 offer marked 'save as to costs'
Whether defendant's open-court statements justified awarding all costs against the successful claimant
Scope of discretion on costs where damages were only £180
linked_authorities: Peter Crouch v King's Healthcare NHS Trust [2004] EWCA Civ 1332

confidence.notes: Permission-only judgment with clear reasoning on costs offers though full appeal outcome is not recorded.

notes: Work stress heart attack appeal; Scott Baker LJ allowed appeal holding employer not put on notice of health risk.

enrichment.short_title: Harding v Pub Estate: employer liability for stress-related heart attack
key_facts: Mr Harding managed the Antelope pub in a rough area for Pub Estate Company, working about 70 hours a week from April 1997.
He suffered a heart attack on 17 September 1998 and was dismissed three days later.
He claimed employers were negligent in exposing him to stress and failing to respond to health complaints.
Judge Gee found liability but the Court of Appeal held complaints did not put employers on notice of impending harm.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from county court judgment finding employers liable for personal injury caused by work-related stress leading to myocardial infarction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; claim dismissed with costs because the employer was never given sufficiently clear warning of a risk to health.
enrichment.ratio: In a first-breakdown stress-at-work case the employee must show plain signs of impending harm to health, not merely stress or environmental complaints; vague or inconsistent complaints to managers, unsupported by medical warnings of heart attack, do not establish foreseeability or breach.
legal_issues: Whether the employer owed and breached a duty to reduce workplace stress
Whether the claimant's complaints put the employer on notice of heart attack risk
Application of Hatton principles to physical rather than psychiatric injury
Whether breach caused or materially contributed to the heart attack
linked_authorities: Hatton v Sutherland [2002] EWCA Civ 76
Barber v Somerset County Council [2004] UKHL 13
Hartman v South Essex Mental Health and Community Care NHS Trust [2005] EWCA Civ 06

confidence.notes: Detailed appellate analysis of complaint evidence and Hatton foreseeability with clear allowance of appeal.

notes: Secure tenancy ground 5 possession appeal; tenant's mother made false exchange statement without daughter's instigation.

enrichment.short_title: Merton v Richards: secure tenancy possession and ground 5 false statement
key_facts: Mrs Richards obtained a secure tenancy at 29 Oxford Avenue through a mutual exchange with elderly tenant Mrs Mahon.
Mrs Mahon never intended to move to the respondent's former flat; the respondent's mother, a council housing officer, knew this but did not tell her daughter.
Mrs Cowper pleaded guilty to obtaining the tenancy by deception; possession was sought under ground 5 for a false statement inducing the grant.
The recorder found the tenant did not know the exchange was a sham and did not instigate her mother's false statement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal of possession of secure council tenancy based on Housing Act 1985 Schedule 2 ground 5.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; ground 5 was not made out because the tenant did not knowingly make a false statement nor instigate her mother's deception.
enrichment.ratio: Ground 5 requires a false statement made knowingly or recklessly by the tenant or by a person acting at the tenant's instigation; instigation means urging or initiating the false statement itself, and the tenant must know the instigated statement is false.
legal_issues: Whether the tenant knowingly participated in a fraudulent mutual exchange
Construction of 'instigation' in ground 5
Whether the civil standard of proof was correctly applied to fraud allegations
Effect of council tax entries on credibility and inducement
linked_authorities: In re H (Minors) [1996] AC 563

confidence.notes: Full Court of Appeal judgment on fact findings and statutory construction with unanimous dismissal.

notes: Lloyd's Names misfeasance amendment applications; Langley J refused leave to plead tort after Jaffray threshold fraud trial.

enrichment.short_title: Lloyd's v Henderson: refusal to plead misfeasance in public office
key_facts: Non-accepting Lloyd's Names sought to amend long-running premium debt litigation to claim misfeasance in public office against Lloyd's.
A threshold fraud trial in Jaffray had already rejected Names' allegations of fraudulent misrepresentation about asbestos liabilities.
The proposed pleading covered wide regulatory failures including LMX, PA spirals, R&R and EU directives.
Langley J held the new claim arose from different facts, was time-barred under CPR 17.4 and had no realistic prospect of success.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications for permission to amend defences and claims in Commercial Court Lloyd's Names litigation to plead misfeasance in public office.
enrichment.outcome: All amendment applications refused on limitation, merits and case-management grounds; Lloyd's was not a public officer and bad faith had already been rejected in Jaffray.
enrichment.ratio: A post-Jaffray misfeasance claim by Lloyd's Names does not arise from the same or substantially the same facts as the threshold fraud issue; Lloyd's is not a public officer for the tort, and late amendment alleging bad faith after a binding fraud trial is an abuse of the court's process.
legal_issues: Whether Lloyd's is a public officer amenable to misfeasance in public office
Whether CPR 17.4 permitted amendment after expiry of limitation
Whether the claim duplicated or circumvented Jaffray fraud findings
Whether the proposed pleading disclosed a realistic cause of action
